speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance regarding the recent strengthening of the Singapore Dollar (a) what is the expected time lag for this adjustment to have a visible effect on exchange rates; (b) what is the effect of global shifts away from the US Dollar on the S$ Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (S$NEER) index basket's currency weighting; and (c) how do these changes impact the Singapore Dollar's stability over time.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development, and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The United States (US) dollar continues to be the major currency used in international trade, including for most commodities, and the US is one of Singapore's largest trading partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development, and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The diversified currency composition of the S$NEER basket reflects the pattern of Singapore's trade with its main import sources and export markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development, and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: These are structural factors that only evolve gradually over time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the US dollar remains dominant, some economists have suggested that the global monetary system may gradually become more fragmented and multi-polar over time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given that Singapore relies heavily on exports and use the exchange rate to manage inflation, could the Minister of State explain how such global currency shifts may affect the Government's ability to keep imported cost stable for Singaporeans, particularly in essentials, such as food, energy and daily necessities?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If you take international trade and if you look at which currency is the invoicing currency, the US dollar, in fact, is used by many countries as the invoicing currency of international trade.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, many commodity prices, like oil and gold, are denominated and still are denominated in the US dollar.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, if you think from a larger perspective, the US dollar continues to be dominant.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And that has the effect of dampening imported inflation in Singapore and a downstream impact on our economy.
